questions.stem: A client who started sertraline 3 weeks ago was prescribed tramadol for back pain 2 days ago. The client is now agitated and sweating, with a temperature of 39 °C (102.2 °F), heart rate 118/min, diarrhea, muscle twitching and rhythmic jerking at both ankles. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Serotonin syndrome
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Anticholinergic toxicity
Alcohol withdrawal

rationale.correct: Serotonin syndrome: mental-status change, autonomic instability and neuromuscular excitability (clonus, hyperreflexia) after serotonergic drugs are combined. Stop the drugs and give supportive care.

perOption.a: Two serotonergic drugs together cause agitation, hyperthermia, diarrhea, clonus and hyperreflexia.
perOption.b: NMS follows antipsychotics and causes lead-pipe rigidity and slow reflexes, not clonus.
perOption.c: This causes hot, dry skin and constipation, not sweating, diarrhea and clonus.
perOption.d: Withdrawal causes tremor and sweating, but clonus with a new serotonergic drug points to serotonin syndrome.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with major depression started fluoxetine 20 mg daily 8 days ago. The client says, "I feel exactly the same, so I'm going to stop taking it." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "It can take 2 to 6 weeks to work fully, so keep taking it and tell your provider."
"A week is long enough to judge, so ask your provider to switch you to a different medicine."
"You can stop it, but lower the dose over a few days first so you don't get side effects."
"Taking it at bedtime instead of in the morning will help it start working faster."

rationale.correct: Antidepressants take 2 to 6 weeks to show full effect. Watch for suicidal thinking early in treatment, and do not stop abruptly.

perOption.a: SSRIs take weeks to work; stopping early means the client never gets the benefit.
perOption.b: One week is too soon to judge an antidepressant.
perOption.c: Tapering matters when stopping, but the medication has not had time to work.
perOption.d: Timing does not speed the onset, and fluoxetine is usually taken in the morning because it can cause insomnia.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach about the delayed effect of SSRIs.

questions.stem: A client taking phenelzine, a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, is choosing meals from the hospital menu. Which meal choice shows that the client needs more teaching?

options.text: Pepperoni pizza with aged parmesan and a glass of tap beer
Grilled fresh chicken with white rice and steamed green beans
Cottage cheese with fresh peaches and a slice of whole-wheat toast
Scrambled eggs with toast and a glass of milk

rationale.correct: With MAOIs, avoid tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, cured or fermented meats, tap beer, soy sauce, sauerkraut) and many drugs, including other antidepressants and decongestants.

perOption.a: Cured meats, aged cheese and tap beer are high in tyramine and can cause a hypertensive crisis with MAOIs.
perOption.b: Fresh meat and fresh vegetables are low in tyramine.
perOption.c: Fresh, unaged cheeses such as cottage cheese are low in tyramine.
perOption.d: Eggs and fresh milk are safe with MAOIs.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client with bipolar disorder who takes lithium 600 mg three times a day has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days. The client has coarse hand tremors and is confused. The lithium level drawn this morning is 2.1 mEq/L. The next dose is due now. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the lithium and notify the provider right away
Give the dose, and recheck the level in 12 hours as planned
Encourage extra salt and 3 L of fluid, then recheck the level
Give the PRN antiemetic and reassess the client in an hour

rationale.correct: Lithium's therapeutic range is about 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L. Vomiting, diarrhea and dehydration raise the level; coarse tremor and confusion mean toxicity, so hold the drug and notify the provider.

perOption.a: A level above about 1.5 mEq/L with confusion and coarse tremor is toxicity; the drug is stopped and the provider decides on treatment.
perOption.c: Fluids and sodium help clear lithium, but the drug is held and the provider notified first.
perOption.d: Treating the vomiting misses the cause and delays care.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who is starting lithium for bipolar disorder and works outdoors in the summer. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.text: "I'll keep my salt and fluid intake about the same every day."
"I'll switch to a low-salt diet to help bring my blood pressure down."
"I'll take ibuprofen when I get headaches after work."
"Once my level is stable, I won't need more blood tests."

rationale.correct: Lithium safety: steady sodium and fluid intake, extra fluids in heat or exercise, no NSAIDs or new diuretics without the provider, and regular levels.

perOption.a: Changes in sodium and fluid alter how much lithium the kidneys clear.
perOption.b: Low sodium makes the kidneys keep lithium, raising the level.
perOption.c: NSAIDs reduce lithium clearance and raise the level.
perOption.d: Levels are checked regularly for as long as the client takes lithium.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client started haloperidol 2 days ago for acute psychosis. The client now has a temperature of 40 °C (104 °F), stiff, rigid muscles, confusion, heavy sweating and a blood pressure that swings between 90/50 and 170/100. The creatine kinase is very high. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome
Acute dystonic reaction
Malignant hyperthermia

rationale.correct: NMS is a medical emergency: stop the antipsychotic, cool the client, support vital signs and expect dantrolene or bromocriptine.

perOption.a: Hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, altered mental status and unstable vital signs after an antipsychotic suggest NMS.
perOption.b: Serotonin syndrome follows serotonergic drugs and causes clonus and hyperreflexia rather than rigidity.
perOption.c: Dystonia causes sudden muscle spasms without fever or unstable vital signs.
perOption.d: Malignant hyperthermia follows certain anesthetics, not antipsychotics.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing four clients who take antipsychotic medications on a psychiatric unit. For each finding, choose the adverse effect it shows.

rows.text: Sudden, painful neck spasm with the eyes rolled upward 6 hours after the first dose
Inner restlessness and constant pacing during the first weeks of treatment
Shuffling gait, hand tremor and a masklike face
Lip smacking and tongue thrusting after years of treatment

rationale.correct: Acute dystonia is treated with an anticholinergic such as diphenhydramine or benztropine. Screen for tardive dyskinesia with the AIMS.

perOption.r1:c1: This is an acute dystonic reaction.
perOption.r1:c3: This is a sudden spasm, not tremor or rigidity.
perOption.r2:c1: This is not a muscle spasm.
perOption.r2:c2: Akathisia is restlessness and an inability to sit still.
perOption.r2:c3: This is not tremor or rigidity.
perOption.r2:c4: This is not involuntary facial movement.
perOption.r4:c4: TD causes involuntary facial movements after long-term use.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has taken clozapine for 2 months. The client reports a sore throat and has a temperature of 38.4 °C (101.1 °F). The evening clozapine dose is due. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the dose and request a CBC with an absolute neutrophil count
Give acetaminophen for the fever and give the clozapine as scheduled
Draw a clozapine level and give the dose if the level is in range
Get a throat swab for streptococcus and keep giving the clozapine

rationale.correct: Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis. Any sign of infection means hold the dose and check the absolute neutrophil count; also watch for seizures, myocarditis and metabolic effects.

perOption.a: Fever and sore throat can be the first signs of clozapine-induced agranulocytosis.
perOption.b: Treating the fever could hide a dangerous drop in neutrophils.
perOption.c: The drug level does not show agranulocytosis; the neutrophil count does.
perOption.d: A swab may be useful, but the neutrophil count comes first and the dose is held.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A 34-year-old client with schizophrenia is starting olanzapine. The client's body mass index is 29 and the client's father has type 2 diabetes. What monitoring should the nurse include in the plan of care?

options.text: Weight, waist size, fasting glucose and lipids
Weekly absolute neutrophil counts for 6 months
Serum drug levels before each dose increase
An ECG before each dose to watch the QT interval

rationale.correct: Atypical antipsychotics, especially olanzapine and clozapine, need metabolic monitoring: weight, waist, glucose and lipids.

perOption.a: Second-generation antipsychotics such as olanzapine cause weight gain, diabetes and high lipids.
perOption.b: Routine ANC monitoring is required for clozapine, not olanzapine.
perOption.c: Olanzapine does not need routine drug levels, unlike lithium.
perOption.d: A baseline ECG may be done, but metabolic monitoring is the main need with olanzapine.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client with major depression told the nurse last week, "Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me." The provider has just prescribed a 90-day supply of amitriptyline. What is the nurse's main safety concern?

options.text: A large supply of a tricyclic can be fatal in overdose because of dysrhythmias
Amitriptyline causes constipation and urinary retention from anticholinergic effects
Amitriptyline causes orthostatic hypotension, which can lead to falls
Amitriptyline causes weight gain, which may worsen the client's self-image

rationale.correct: Tricyclic antidepressants are highly lethal in overdose. Limit the supply for clients at risk of suicide, and watch for anticholinergic effects and orthostatic hypotension.

perOption.a: TCA overdose causes fatal dysrhythmias and seizures, so a client with suicidal thoughts should get small supplies.
perOption.b: These are common effects, but they are not the main risk for this client.
perOption.c: This is a real risk, but it is less urgent than overdose in a client with suicidal thoughts.
perOption.d: Weight gain is common but is not a safety concern.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client who has taken valproic acid for bipolar disorder for 2 months reports fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea and upper abdominal pain that goes through to the back. The nurse notes yellowing of the sclera. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Liver toxicity or pancreatitis from the valproate
Expected stomach upset from the start of therapy
High ammonia levels caused by the valproic acid itself
Lithium toxicity from a drug interaction

rationale.correct: Valproate needs liver tests and platelet counts; watch for hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis and hyperammonemia, and avoid it in pregnancy because it causes birth defects.

perOption.a: Valproate can cause hepatotoxicity and pancreatitis; jaundice and pain radiating to the back point to these.
perOption.b: Jaundice and severe abdominal pain are not expected effects.
perOption.c: Hyperammonemia causes confusion and lethargy, not jaundice and abdominal pain.
perOption.d: The client is not taking lithium.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client started lamotrigine 25 mg daily for bipolar depression 10 days ago. The nurse is reviewing what to report. Which finding should the client report to the provider right away?

options.text: A new rash anywhere on the body
A mild headache in the morning
Some dizziness when standing up
Blurred vision when tired at night

rationale.correct: Lamotrigine is increased slowly to reduce the risk of severe rash, and any new rash is reported at once.

perOption.a: Lamotrigine can cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome; any new rash must be evaluated before the next dose.
perOption.b: Headache is a common, minor effect.
perOption.c: Mild dizziness is common; the client rises slowly.
perOption.d: Visual blurring can occur and should be mentioned, but it is not an emergency.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: An 84-year-old client with benign prostatic hyperplasia and mild memory loss is admitted for pneumonia. The provider prescribes diphenhydramine 50 mg at bedtime for sleep. Why should the nurse question this prescription?

options.text: Its anticholinergic effects cause confusion, urinary retention and falls
It raises blood glucose and can make the client's pneumonia harder to treat
It causes rebound high blood pressure when it is stopped after a few days
It does not work well as a sleep aid in clients over 80

rationale.correct: Avoid strongly anticholinergic drugs in older adults: they cause confusion, urinary retention, constipation and falls.

perOption.a: Diphenhydramine is on the Beers list of drugs to avoid in older adults, especially with BPH and cognitive impairment.
perOption.b: Diphenhydramine does not raise glucose or worsen pneumonia.
perOption.c: This is not a known effect of diphenhydramine.
perOption.d: The concern is harm, not effectiveness.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize risky medications for older adults.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client takes ibuprofen 800 mg three times a day for knee osteoarthritis. At a clinic visit, which finding should the nurse report to the provider right away?

options.text: Black, tarry stools for the last 2 days
Heartburn after doses that is eased by an antacid
Knee stiffness for 20 minutes after waking up
Mild nausea when a dose is taken without food

rationale.correct: NSAIDs can cause GI bleeding, kidney injury, high blood pressure and cardiovascular events, especially in older adults.

perOption.a: Black stools suggest upper GI bleeding, a serious NSAID adverse effect.
perOption.b: Dyspepsia should be discussed, but it is not an emergency.
perOption.c: Brief morning stiffness is expected with osteoarthritis.
perOption.d: This improves when the dose is taken with food.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who uses acetaminophen for chronic back pain and drinks two or three beers most evenings. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.text: "I'll check cold and sleep medicine labels for acetaminophen too."
"It's sold over the counter, so I can take up to 6 grams a day."
"A few beers in the evening won't matter with acetaminophen."
"If my pain is bad, I'll take an extra dose on top of the usual."

rationale.correct: Acetaminophen: usually no more than 3 to 4 g a day for healthy adults, less with liver disease or regular alcohol use; watch for hidden sources.

perOption.a: Hidden acetaminophen in combination products is a common cause of accidental overdose.
perOption.b: The usual adult maximum is 3 to 4 g a day, and lower with regular alcohol use.
perOption.c: Regular alcohol use raises the risk of liver injury.
perOption.d: Doses must stay within the daily limit.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client with heart failure takes lisinopril 20 mg and spironolactone 25 mg daily. The client's potassium is now 6.0 mEq/L, and the creatinine is unchanged. Which explanation of the high potassium is most accurate?

options.text: Both drugs reduce how much potassium the kidneys excrete
Lisinopril shifts potassium out of cells into the blood
Spironolactone increases potassium absorption from the gut
The client's low-sodium diet is raising the potassium

rationale.correct: ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium-sparing diuretics all make the kidneys keep potassium; watch potassium closely when they are combined.

perOption.a: ACE inhibitors lower aldosterone, and spironolactone blocks it; together they make the kidneys keep potassium.
perOption.b: ACE inhibitors raise potassium through less excretion, not a shift out of cells.
perOption.c: Spironolactone acts on the kidney, not the gut.
perOption.d: Salt substitutes containing potassium can, but a low-sodium diet alone does not.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize drug combinations that cause hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: A client who takes warfarin 5 mg daily for a mechanical heart valve is prescribed ciprofloxacin for 7 days for a urinary tract infection. The client's INR last week was 2.8. What should the nurse monitor more closely?

options.text: INR and signs of bleeding
Blood glucose levels
Hearing and balance
Thyroid function tests

rationale.correct: Check for interactions whenever a new drug is added to warfarin, and expect closer INR monitoring.

perOption.a: Many antibiotics, including ciprofloxacin, increase warfarin's effect.
perOption.b: Fluoroquinolones can affect glucose, but the main concern here is bleeding.
perOption.c: Ototoxicity is linked with aminoglycosides, not ciprofloxacin.
perOption.d: This interaction does not involve the thyroid.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client who takes simvastatin 40 mg every evening tells the nurse, "I've started drinking a big glass of grapefruit juice every morning." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Grapefruit can raise simvastatin levels and the risk of muscle damage."
"Grapefruit makes simvastatin less effective at lowering cholesterol."
"That's fine, as long as you take the juice and the pill 12 hours apart."
"Grapefruit juice helps the body absorb simvastatin more evenly."

rationale.correct: Grapefruit interacts with some statins, calcium channel blockers and immunosuppressants by blocking CYP3A4.

perOption.a: Grapefruit inhibits CYP3A4, which breaks down simvastatin, so levels and the risk of myopathy rise.
perOption.b: Grapefruit raises simvastatin levels; it does not lower them.
perOption.c: The enzyme effect lasts more than a day, so spacing does not prevent the interaction.
perOption.d: Higher absorption is the problem, not a benefit.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: Two weeks after starting allopurinol for gout, a client comes to the clinic with a fever, a painful rash with blisters spreading across the chest and back, peeling skin, and sores in the mouth and on the lips. The client also takes hydrochlorothiazide. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Allergic contact dermatitis
Acute gout flare
Disseminated herpes zoster

rationale.correct: SJS is an emergency: stop the drug and get emergency care. It is linked to allopurinol, sulfonamides, lamotrigine and several antiseizure drugs.

perOption.a: Fever, blistering rash, skin detachment and mucosal sores after a new drug suggest SJS.
perOption.b: Contact dermatitis stays where the skin touched the irritant and does not cause fever or mouth sores.
perOption.c: Gout causes a hot, swollen joint, not a widespread blistering rash.
perOption.d: Zoster follows a dermatome or spreads as vesicles, without widespread peeling and mucosal sores.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client in the psychiatric emergency department is shouting and throwing chairs. The provider prescribes haloperidol 5 mg IM and lorazepam 2 mg IM, which the nurse gives. Twenty minutes later the client is asleep in a quiet room. What is the nurse's priority now?

options.text: Monitor airway, breathing, blood pressure and level of sedation
Leave the client undisturbed in the quiet room until the client wakes
Give a second dose in 15 minutes so the client does not wake agitated
Begin teaching about the medications so the client accepts them next time

rationale.correct: After emergency sedation, monitor airway, vital signs, sedation level and extrapyramidal effects closely.

perOption.a: The combination can cause deep sedation, hypotension and respiratory depression.
perOption.b: A sedated client needs regular checks.
perOption.d: Teaching can wait until the client is awake and calm.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
